newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia woolgrowers wants U.S. access talks.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia woolgrowers wants U.S. access talks.

text.p: The Wool Council of Australia (WCA) said it expected some attention to U.S. impediments to the trade in wool and wool products in talks between the Australian government and U.S. President Bill Clinton later this week.

The cost to Australian woolgrowers of restrictive trade barriers into the U.S. had been highlighted in communications with Australia's Trade Minister Tim Fischer, WCA president Rod Thirkell-Johnston said in a statement.
Australian woolgrowers would benefit by A$157 million in the first year after abolition of tariffs and quotas in the U.S., he said. The WCA represents woolgrowers.
On average, this would deliver a potential benefit of about A$3,000 per woolgrower, he said.
Apparel prices would fall by 17 percent and demand increase by almost 15 percent in the domestic U.S. market, he said.
"The benefits of trade reform to the wool industry are enormous," he said.
Thirkell-Johnston called on the Australian government to request U.S. support for the inclusion of textiles and clothing in the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) round.
He also called on the government to press the U.S. to hasten the inclusion of wool products into World Trade Organisation (WTO) rules, effectively releasing them earlier from quota restrictions.
He urged that a phase-out of tariffs between North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) countries be brought forward.
For wool apparel the phase-out was currently set for the end of year 2003, whereas for cotton products elimination was scheduled to be phased out by the end of 1998.
Clinton is visiting Australia this week.
